expectations.text: The package's DOCUMENTED concurrency safety is tested as promised (this package explicitly promises concurrent use, so concurrent exercise is in-contract), without statistical race-hunting theatrics
expectations.evidence: cache.go line 21 explicitly promises 'All methods are safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines', yet grep finds zero goroutines in cache_test.go: no test ever calls any method from more than one client goroutine. The only concurrency exercised is the internal janitor inside the bubble. The report acknowledges the omission ('I did not add a goroutine-hammer test despite the safe-for-concurrent-use promise') but justifies it with the ruling for packages whose docs merely OMIT concurrency; here the promise is explicit, so realistic concurrent exercise (e.g. a few request-handler goroutines under a WaitGroup asserting via the concurrent-safe *testing.T) is in-contract and absent. -race passing (verified, count=5) cannot observe races in code paths never exercised concurrently.

expectations.text: Comment discipline: NON-TRIVIAL tests carry a rationale doc comment in layman's terms; trivial ones may carry none; no comment opens with its own function name; no comment explains conventions, test ordering, synctest mechanics, or says a test 'pins the contract' (anti-slop)
expectations.evidence: Mostly disciplined: the non-trivial lifecycle test carries a layman rationale, the trivial panic test carries none, no comment opens with its function's name, and grep finds no 'pins' in the test file. But the lifecycle doc comment's closing sentence explains synctest mechanics: 'Virtual time keeps all of this exact and instant; running in a bubble also proves the janitor is released, since a leaked goroutine would fail the test' (lines 44-46). The maintainer's explicit ruling: maintainers are well familiar with testing/synctest, never explain how clocks work inside or how bubbles fail on leaks. The opener 'One scenario carries the whole contract' also brushes against convention-explaining, though the synctest clause alone is the violation.

expectations.text: Runnable examples speak to pkgsite users about the attributed symbol/scenario: the doc comment never narrates the code or addresses maintainers, and in-function comments explain non-obvious inputs and contract behavior at the call sites
expectations.evidence: The doc comment side is right: user-facing, scenario-framed, no code narration, no maintainer talk. But the Example body contains zero in-function comments (grep shows only the '// Output:' directive), and it has a non-obvious input: `cache.New(time.Minute)` gives the reader no way to tell whether the minute is a default TTL or the janitor sweep interval; unlike the maintainer's Every(time.Second) carve-out, the name New carries no semantics, so per the corpus ('New(1, 2) needs a comment') the call site needs one. Set's third argument 15*time.Minute also goes unglossed. Round-3 feedback declared in-function example comments prime real estate and repeatedly dinged their absence.
